title: Prisons, probation and access to justice
label: 11 November 2026 · Ministry of Justice
summary: Lord Chancellor Alex Norris discussed prison overcrowding, rehabilitation, probation staffing and electronic monitoring, as well as support for victims, access to legal advice and the independence of judges. He said new sentencing arrangements and investment should ease pressure, but committee members questioned whether probation supervision and tagging offer enough protection, and challenged delays and failures in prison services. Norris accepted that some problems remain, while arguing that limited capacity and past underinvestment constrain what can be delivered.

speakers.label: Chair
speakers.name: Lord Foster of Bath
speakers.role: Chair of the Justice and Home Affairs Committee

speakers.label: Alex Norris
speakers.name: The Rt Hon Alex Norris MP
speakers.role: Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice, Ministry of Justice

glossary.definition: The legislation changing how prison sentences are served, including the time spent in prison and in the community.
Sending someone back to prison after release, usually because they have broken their release conditions.
Conditions a person must follow after leaving prison; breaking them can lead to being returned to prison.
The public service that supervises people serving sentences in the community or released from prison.
The independent body that selects candidates for judicial jobs, rather than leaving the choice to politicians.
Community members who hear many less serious criminal cases, usually alongside a trained legal adviser.
The 2012 law that changed who could receive publicly funded legal help and which types of case qualified.
Public funding that helps people who cannot afford it get legal advice or representation.
The UK regulator responsible for overseeing areas including online safety and communications.
A UK law that requires online services to take steps to address illegal and harmful material.
Non-disclosure agreements: contracts that restrict people from sharing specified information.
Legal cases brought mainly to intimidate or silence people who speak out on matters of public interest.
A legal rule that can prevent the Crown, including government bodies, from being prosecuted in some circumstances.

chapters.title: Prison pressure and rehabilitation
chapters.takeaway: Norris said overcrowding has made rehabilitation harder, while members pressed for more practical changes and questioned whether further reviews are needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are the biggest challenges facing the Ministry of Justice?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: The urgent pressures are a shortage of prison places and growing delays in the courts. The new sentencing arrangements and the Courts and Tribunals Bill are intended to ease those pressures and help the system focus again on reducing reoffending.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I also want the department to support the legal sector, which is worth about £40 billion to the economy, and to protect the independence of judges.

turns.speaker: Lord Empey
turns.text: People leaving prison still reoffend at high rates. How can more of their time be spent on education, treatment and other activities that help them avoid crime?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Overcrowding makes it much harder to get people to treatment for drugs or alcohol, mental health support, education and programmes that address offending. That can leave people less prepared to return to the community, and the number sent back to prison after release has doubled in a decade.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: There are examples of progress. At HMP Cardiff, staff start supporting people from their first day, even though many are there only briefly. The share of people who served at least a year and were working six months after release rose from 15% in 2021 to 40% now.

turns.speaker: Lord Empey
turns.text: Prison governors have too little freedom to make basic decisions. Some can’t approve spending over £500. Will you review those limits?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I don’t want to micromanage local purchases. Governors have told me that limits can delay essential equipment, such as washing machines, or push them to buy cheaper items that wear out quickly. I’m comparing public and private prisons and will look again at the rules.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: People also need mental health and addiction support to continue when they leave prison. Would you support better links between prison care and local services?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Yes. Ideally, people could continue with the same treatment provider after release. That isn’t always possible because local services differ and people may leave prison for a different area. But housing, work, relationships and treatment should be arranged as early as possible, ideally months before release.

turns.speaker: Lord Dubs
turns.text: How will you deal with the shortage of prison places? And do we really need another review when earlier reports have already identified the problems?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: We’re committed to building 14,000 more places by 2031, at a cost of £5 billion; 3,300 have been built. The sentencing changes are also intended to reduce the pressure on cells while keeping people under controls in the community.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Independent reviews can help a new minister hear a range of advice, but they must lead to action. Recommendations from earlier reviews have informed policy and legislation; they don’t automatically become law.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Reports have repeatedly called for more prison education, yet education capacity has fallen. The Government agreed with many recommendations but cut the education budget. Why wait for another report?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I don’t accept that nothing has been done. The prison estate is so stretched that it limits what education and other services can provide. The education budget hasn’t been cut, but rising costs have reduced what it can buy. I want more prisoners attending and completing classes.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: The sentencing changes are now in force and are meant to create room to improve provision. I hope the current review will help identify what should happen next as the system moves out of crisis.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You call the change a progression model, but it looks like a return to the old system: a third of a sentence in prison, then time in the community. Was it a mistake to call it early release?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I avoid that phrase. The aim is to replace repeated emergency releases with a permanent change to how sentences are served, so the prison system can plan. But the public mainly want to know who is leaving and when.

chapters.title: Probation: workload and supervision
chapters.takeaway: Norris promised better pay and lower workloads, but Baroness Hughes challenged whether reduced active contact still counts as meaningful supervision.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hughes of Stretford
turns.text: Probation staff have faced vacancies, heavy caseloads and years of change. More money alone won’t fix that. What are you doing about staffing and workload?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Probation has been underappreciated, despite the vital work its staff do. I’ve promised better pay and less work: staff received a 6% rise last year, and the offer this year is 5%, pending a staff vote.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: We’ve committed to reducing workloads by 25% by spring, partly by filling vacancies. The number of probation officers is up 6% year on year, and recruitment is ahead of target. We also use software to transcribe probation meetings, so officers can focus more on speaking with the person.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hughes of Stretford
turns.text: The Probation Reset programme means someone on a 12-month community order may have active contact with an officer for only 16 weeks. After that, there may be no routine contact. Is that what the public think supervision means?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: The amount of active contact is intended to depend on a person’s risks and progress. Licence conditions can continue after regular meetings stop, and breaking them can bring sanctions, including recall to prison.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hughes of Stretford
turns.text: But after those 16 weeks, contact can stop unless a breach comes to light. People may think an offender is being watched when there’s actually no regular contact.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I believe people are still subject to effective controls and can be sanctioned if they break their conditions. That’s the balance we’re aiming for.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hughes of Stretford
turns.text: Many new recruits have little experience, while experienced staff have left. Will you invest in training and help rebuild that experience?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: The service has lost many mid-career staff, so newer officers have fewer experienced colleagues to learn from. There’s no shortcut to experience, but we provide training at the start and throughout people’s careers. We’re also considering whether probation’s structure should change, while being careful not to unsettle a fragile workforce.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You say the workforce is fragile. Is the prison and probation service itself partly to blame, or has the problem been government funding?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I have confidence in the service. It has made the best of the staff and resources available. Governments decide the funding; the service is responsible for putting its staff in the right places and training them.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are you confident that the £700 million over four years is enough, given that more people are still leaving probation than joining?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Yes, I believe it gives us the resources for a long-term recovery. Keeping staff matters as much as recruiting them, so we’re working on pay and workloads as well as hiring.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hughes of Stretford
turns.text: Would you consider aligning probation areas with elected mayors and local authorities? Greater Manchester’s regional arrangement helped connect probation with prisons, housing, health and employment services.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Yes. People often point to the Manchester model as a useful example, and I’m going there to hear more about it.

chapters.title: Electronic monitoring and victim safety
chapters.takeaway: Norris agreed that tags must be fitted reliably and victims properly supported, but said monitoring and release conditions can’t guarantee constant real-time intervention.

turns.speaker: Baroness Buscombe
turns.text: We were told that only 55% of GPS and radio tags are fitted properly, and about one in five people wait more than two weeks. Why are people still leaving prison without tags, and why is fitting them before release only a pilot?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: There’s a long history of problems with electronic monitoring. We’ve introduced a presumption that people will be tagged, though not everyone can be—for example, some people have health needs or no suitable fixed address. The figures should show a substantial increase under the new sentencing arrangements.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: A tag is useful only if it’s actually fitted. Fitting it before someone leaves prison has worked better in the pilot prisons, and I’m committed to making that more common. Home equipment may still need to be installed after release.

turns.speaker: Baroness Buscombe
turns.text: What happens to people with no settled address? Are they found and returned to prison if they disappear?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: People released on a licence without housing are offered accommodation, ideally through local authorities. Emergency accommodation can be provided for up to 84 days, and some people must live in approved premises. We try to plan housing months before release.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: A particular concern is people who leave court unexpectedly, such as after a sentence already served or an acquittal. They may have lost their home and aren’t required to stay in contact with probation. We’re working with councils to find them somewhere to go.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How much of the £700 million is going to housing for people leaving prison?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I can’t give you the amount today. That funding has supported emergency accommodation, and other government housing money is also being used for vulnerable groups. I’ll send the committee the figure.

turns.speaker: Baroness Berridge
turns.text: Serco’s past dealings with the Serious Fraud Office raise questions about the Ministry’s electronic-monitoring contract. How can you uphold the rule of law while managing a contract with that history?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: We inherited contracts that run to the end of this decade, and we must honour them. My immediate job is to get the best performance from the current contract. If a contractor were found to have committed fraud, I’d expect there to be a way to end the contract.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’ve suggested bringing tagging in-house or opening it up to more providers. Are you studying whether the service should be brought in-house?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: We support bringing services back into public hands when that gives better value and results. But we’re not studying it yet; we need to make the current contract work before deciding what should replace it.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bertin
turns.text: Domestic abuse groups are worried that perpetrators have been released under the new arrangements. The Government wanted to exclude more domestic-abuse cases, but didn’t. Why?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: We would have liked to exclude more cases, but domestic abuse isn’t a single offence, which made that difficult. We were able to exclude people convicted of child sex offences, rape and killing someone, but I accept we didn’t go as far as we wanted on domestic abuse.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bertin
turns.text: Could high-risk perpetrators be monitored more actively, with an immediate alert if they enter an area where they shouldn’t be? We were told that breaches outside office hours may not be dealt with until the next morning.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: In a small number of the highest-risk cases, more immediate monitoring may be possible. But tagging isn’t a guarantee of instant intervention. It can provide clear evidence of a breach, which must then be followed up.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bertin
turns.text: Do all known victims get contacted before the person who harmed them is released?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I’ve committed to contacting everyone in the victim contact scheme and giving them a chance to contribute to release conditions. The aim is for conditions to fit around the survivor’s life, not force the survivor to fit around the perpetrator. We’ve added a helpline and support for local services, but the real test is how victims experience it.

chapters.title: Violence against women and harmful online material
chapters.takeaway: The committee pressed for stronger enforcement of protections for victims and laws against harmful sexual material online.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bertin
turns.text: The Government has changed laws on harmful pornography, but people can still find rape-related material through search engines, sometimes without an age check. How will the laws be enforced?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Passing laws isn’t enough if people can still find the material. The Online Safety Act sets rules for online services, and Ofcom is working with search engines to close gaps when they’re found. The online environment changes quickly, so enforcement needs to keep adapting.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bertin
turns.text: Legal pornography sites should follow the law, and search engines shouldn’t make illegal content so easy to find. The Government needs to put much more pressure on them.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I accept that challenge. Ofcom and the Government are engaging with those companies, but it’s for us to show that the rules are working.

chapters.title: Legal advice, judges and court services
chapters.takeaway: Norris backed rebuilding access to legal advice and protecting independent judicial appointments, while members highlighted shortages and practical barriers in courts.

turns.speaker: Lord Bach
turns.text: The LASPO Act left many people unable to get legal advice on housing, debt, benefits, immigration or family problems. What will you do to repair that loss?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I accept that access to advice has been badly weakened. We’re putting money in now, including £25 million for legal support, but that’s only the first step. We need to rebuild a network of advice services and law centres so people can get help early, before a problem becomes a court case.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: People increasingly turn to automated tools for answers, but that doesn’t replace good legal advice. We need to work out how local advice, online services and formal legal processes can guide people to the right help.

turns.speaker: Lord Bach
turns.text: Law centres are closing or at risk of closing. If more disappear, the situation will get worse. Do you agree?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Yes. The immediate funding is intended to stop services being lost while we work out how to rebuild the wider system.

turns.speaker: Lord Anderson of Ipswich
turns.text: Would you consider abolishing the Judicial Appointments Commission and giving ministers the power to choose judges? Independent appointments protect the courts from political interference.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: No. Judges must be able to decide cases without political pressure. That independence helps protect our freedoms and gives people confidence in our courts. It would be a terrible idea to give politicians that power.

turns.speaker: Baroness Berridge
turns.text: There are too few magistrates, judges and court staff. London courts aren’t always running at full capacity because there aren’t enough judges. What are you doing?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Magistrate numbers fell from 29,000 in 2010 to 12,000 in 2022, but have risen to around 15,000 or 16,000. Recruitment is going well. Some people assume they need legal training or don’t have time, so we’re trying to correct those misunderstandings.

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: We’ve removed limits on how many days judges can sit, and they’ve handled more work than expected. We’re also recruiting more legal advisers for magistrates’ courts. Court ushers and clerks matter too, and I believe we have enough of them at present.

turns.speaker: Baroness Berridge
turns.text: Jurors can be required to serve but may receive only £64.95 a day, paid afterwards. Some can’t afford travel to court the next day. Could you look at paying expenses in advance?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: The allowances haven’t kept pace with the cost of living. I’ll examine the committee’s evidence and consider how to make the experience fairer for people who are required to serve.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Parliament required a report on how coroners should investigate stillbirths, but seven years later the answer is still that it’ll come ‘in due course’. Is that acceptable?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: No. I’ll look into the delay. Parliament required the report, and the public deserve more than an open-ended promise.

chapters.title: Prison safety and accountability
chapters.takeaway: The Chair challenged the department over missed fire-safety commitments and whether current scrutiny is enough to hold public prisons to account.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Government said automatic fire detection would be fitted in all public prisons by 2027, but now says that won’t happen and hasn’t given us a clear alternative plan. Is that acceptable?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: The responsibility is mine. The prison estate is old, underinvested in and crowded, so safety work has to be planned without closing too many cells. We’re spending another £275 million on fire safety this year, but the original timetable wasn’t deliverable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Those pressures were known when the 2027 deadline was set. Why should we have confidence that the department planned properly?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I understand the frustration. Years of underinvestment and the need to keep enough cells open made the plan harder to deliver than expected. I accept responsibility for changing the timetable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Public prisons have Crown immunity, which can make it hard to prosecute when things go wrong. Should that be reviewed so responsibility is clearer?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: I believe there are already strong ways to scrutinise prisons, including independent inspection and parliamentary committees. I don’t think removing Crown immunity would materially improve that accountability.

turns.speaker: Lord Dubs
turns.text: Are you concerned that powerful people are using court cases to silence those who speak about abuse?

turns.speaker: Alex Norris
turns.text: Yes. We’ve changed the law so non-disclosure agreements can’t be used to hide sexual misconduct, and I’m working with John Whittingdale on a bill to discourage legal cases brought to silence people. The rules must protect a fair balance, not be abused.
